author: Dante
title: Three voices in Hell
where: *Inferno*, Cantos 3, 5 and 26
why: The chain of rhyme hands each middle sound on: here it rhymes pain, maker and love, and the rhyme the gate leaves open is completed after it; to an Italian, Auden wrote, parting Dante’s matter from this form is unthinkable.

author: Dante
title: Three places on the mountain
where: *Purgatorio*, Cantos 15, 17 and 28
why: A question about dividing goods is answered by likening the good to light and the souls to bright bodies that give it back: light is not made less by the number receiving it. Auden copied the closing lines in 1941.

author: Dante
title: The last canto
where: *Paradiso*, Canto 33
why: The three paradoxes name Mary by the event the next lines state outright: in her the maker of human nature became its creature. Such pairs were a formula of the Church’s prayer, and in the poem’s faith each is fact.

author: Aeschylus
title: The yoke, the cloth and the net
where: *Agamemnon*: the first chorus, the king’s return, the murder
why: The king gives one word to both acts, to disobeying and to killing his child, and calls neither the lesser evil; this is the choice Auden gives first for the Greek tragic situation, in which either course is wrong.

author: Sophocles
title: The laws and the city
where: *Antigone*: the elders’ song on man, Antigone’s answer, Creon and his son
why: The elders ask for the land’s laws and the gods’ sworn justice together, a high city for the man who keeps both and none for the man who dares wrong; Auden’s Antigone must fail her brother or her city.

author: Horace
title: A ship, a crossing and a bee
where: *Odes* I.14, I.3 and IV.2
why: The measure is made of the lengths of syllables, a long one counted as two short; the break in the middle of the long line lets a question end one half and a command fill the other.

author: Augustine
title: The restless heart
where: *Confessions*, Books I, II and X
why: Augustine says why he tells God what God knows: he tells it before God to his own kind, to stir up his devotion and theirs, so that all may say the psalm’s praise.

author: Shakespeare
title: Falstaff’s prose, the King’s verse
where: *Henry IV, Part 2*: Act 1, Scene 2; Act 3, Scene 1; Act 5, Scene 5
why: Falstaff twice answers the Chief Justice with the judge’s own words crossed, which makes a wish of one charge and turns the other on the Prince; Auden said he uses word-play on purpose, to be liked and treated kindly.

author: Shakespeare
title: A word said twice
where: *Othello*, Act 3, Scene 3; Act 4, Scene 1; Act 5, Scene 2
why: Iago hands Othello’s words back as questions and commits himself to nothing; the monster, and the conclusion that Iago means something, come from Othello, as in Auden’s account, where Iago need only bring up what is already in Othello’s mind.

author: Shakespeare
title: Three speeches of Hamlet
where: *Hamlet*, Act 1, Scene 2; Act 3, Scene 1; Act 5, Scene 2
why: The sentence lists every outward sign of grief, a line to each, before its last words say what they cannot do; a verb kept to the end holds the sense open until all are named.

author: Shakespeare
title: Ariel’s song
where: *The Tempest*, Act 1, Scene 2, with Act 3, Scene 2 and the Epilogue
why: The song is in the measure of the charms in A Midsummer Night’s Dream and Macbeth, and Auden calls it a spell; the voice leaves the measure most where two stresses slow it on the new word.

author: Ben Jonson
title: The Fox’s gold, song and sentence
where: *Volpone*, Acts 1, 3 and 5
why: Volpone greets his gold in the words of Christian worship, saint, hail, adoration, relic, shrine, so Act 1 opens on a man worshipping money; Auden says a Jonson hero is one of the seven deadly sins.

author: Pascal
title: The heart and the reason
where: *Pensées*, fragments 277 and 278, 347 and 348, and 233
why: One word in two senses credits the heart with reasons and says that reason, the knowing power, does not know them; the clause is an addition in the manuscript, and Auden says Pascal set the heart above the reason.

author: Racine
title: Racine’s line
where: *Phèdre*, Act 1, Scenes 1 and 3, and Act 2, Scene 5
why: The third line is twelve syllables of Phèdre’s parentage and nothing else, and the cut after the sixth sets her father in one half and her mother in the other.

author: Blake
workTitle: The Marriage of Heaven and Hell
title: The voice of the Devil
where: The section of that name, the first “Memorable Fancy” and “Proverbs of Hell”
why: The contraries keep the errors’ nouns, Body, Soul, Energy and Reason, and leave out Evil, Good and God: the third error has God torment man in Eternity, and Auden called an eternal penalty imposed by God a misunderstanding of Hell.

author: Goethe
title: The changing measures of Faust
where: *Faust*, Part I: the Prologue in Heaven, the first Study scene and Gretchen’s room
why: The measure changes where the speaker changes: the archangels keep the four-beat stanza of their hymn, and Mephistopheles, who says he cannot make high words, speaks the mixed rhymed lines in which the Lord then answers him.

author: Kierkegaard
title: Abraham told four ways
where: *Fear and Trembling*: the Preparation, the Panegyric on Abraham and the Preliminary Expectoration, in the English of L. M. Hollander (1923)
why: After each of four retellings of Abraham’s journey comes a paragraph on weaning a child, opened and closed alike: a refrain that marks each telling as one of a set, which is how the narrator describes them.

author: Baudelaire
title: The dandy’s warning
where: *Intimate Journals*: *Rockets*, XIII and XXVI; *My Heart Laid Bare*, LXXII and LXXIX
why: The simile turns I into a man and keeps him, so his pride is told of a third person, by comparison with the passers-by; Auden calls it the dandy’s mistake to seek individuality in being unlike others.

author: Ibsen
title: Two riddles and an onion
where: *Peer Gynt*, Acts 2 and 5
why: The two sayings are built alike, and in Ibsen the commands differ by one added word; the Old Man himself calls it the sundering word.

author: Dostoevsky
title: The Grand Inquisitor
where: *The Brothers Karamazov*, Part II, Book V, Chapter 5
why: Dostoevsky has the old man forbid an answer and supply his own, and has Ivan say so; the old man holds that the Prisoner has no right to add anything, and Auden that he has no need to answer.

author: Rimbaud
title: The experiment and its record
where: *A Season in Hell* (*Une saison en enfer*, 1873): the chapters “Alchemy of the Word” and “Adieu”
why: The steps stand in the past definite, which the grammar of the time keeps for a time completely over: he sets down as closed history what he did to himself.

author: Henry Adams
title: The dynamo and the Virgin
where: *The Education of Henry Adams*, chapters 25, 19 and 1
why: The simile joins machine and Cross by one verb, feel; two sentences later the likeness is gone and one, not he, begins to pray; Auden’s verdict is that Adams worshiped the Dynamo, and the passage itself reports prayer to it.

author: Melville
title: Ishmael and Ahab
where: *Moby-Dick*, Chapters 1, 37 and 128
why: The main clause waits behind four whenever clauses; in two Ishmael finds himself doing things, in the fourth his low spirits and a principle act on him; the main verb means consider; Auden’s Ishmael has consciousness and no will.

author: Rilke
workTitle: The Journal of My Other Self
title: A single line of verse
where: *The Journal of My Other Self* *(The Notebooks of Malte Laurids Brigge)*, Part One, pages 18 to 20 of the edition of 1930; and one poem, “Der Panther”
why: One short assertion carries eleven phrases, each headed by the same word, so the sentence can keep adding to its count before it calls the whole of it not enough; Auden says the passage counts out what one poem requires.

author: Kafka
title: K. and the Castle
where: *The Castle*, chapters 1, 2 and 8, in the English of Willa and Edwin Muir (1930)
why: One sentence says five things of a street, each new one taking back part of the last, and ends no nearer the Castle; Auden cites Kafka’s aphorism that there is a goal and no way, only wavering.

author: T. S. Eliot
title: Furies in the drawing room
where: *The Family Reunion* (1939), the whole play
why: Eliot made a line of three stresses and varying length to bring verse close to the speech of his day; Auden could read no line he tried with fewer than four stresses.

author: Gluck
title: Orpheus calls Eurydice
where: *Orfeo ed Euridice*, Act 3, Scene 1, with Act 1, Scenes 1 and 2
why: Calzabigi writes the aria in the line of eight, since Petrarch’s time a line of religious verse and of verse for music, and its two fixed stresses hold through the cries and stops of the third line.

author: Mozart
title: The catalogue and the duet
where: *Don Giovanni*, Act 1
why: The accents of this line never move, and in the totals all but one fall on a country or a figure, so the regular cadence the reference books describe carries a count, and Auden calls the Don’s pleasure arithmetical.

author: Mozart
title: The trials
where: *The Magic Flute*, Act 2: the questions before the trials, the Queen of the Night’s aria, and the end of the opera
why: One high word asks two men whether they will win by fighting; Tamino takes it up and names his victory and reward, and Papageno refuses it in a bird-catcher’s familiar words: for Auden, the spiritual and the natural.

author: Beethoven
title: Leonore’s answer
where: *Fidelio*, Act 2, Scene 5, with Act 1, Scene 6 and Act 2, Scene 3
why: In the shortened text of two American librettos Leonore’s answer has lost its reason and is a denial said twice, which is how the notes of Auden’s lecture give it, beside Cordelia’s twice-said denial of any cause.

author: Wagner
title: Senta’s ballad
where: *The Flying Dutchman*, Act 2, Scene 1, with lines from Acts 1, 2 and 3
why: The measure is steady while the ballad describes the ship; at the cry Hui the lines begin on the beat, and where he flies like an arrow two syllables, sung as quick notes, come before each beat.

author: Wagner
title: No more Isolde
where: *Tristan und Isolde*, Act 2, Scenes 1 and 2, and the end of Act 3
why: Of the ten verbs two are Isolde’s, both past, and seven are Lady Love’s, who took the deed, turns it and may lead her. Auden in 1941: the lovers’ tie holds no possibilities, being fixed to the potion they drank.

author: Wagner
title: The end foretold
where: *Götterdämmerung*, the Prelude and Act 3, with the English of Margaret Armour (1911)
why: Wagner gave up end-rhyme for the stave of the oldest German verse because, he wrote, it follows the accents of speech and makes one image of the words it joins; here it joins eternal to end.

author: Bizet
title: Carmen’s liberty
where: *Carmen*, Act 1, Scene 5; Act 2, Scenes 5 and 6; Act 3, Scene 2 (the scene numbers of the French libretto)
why: Carmen answers the young men in the eight-syllable line of lyric and lighter verse; the line printed with ten has a word twice; the verses, which Auden says are addressed to the composer, were by Dean’s account the composer’s own.

author: Verdi
title: Violetta alone
where: *La Traviata*, Act 1, Scenes 3 and 5, and the last lines of Act 3
why: Piave closes both stanzas of Violetta’s song on Alfredo’s lines, so what she has just said, that his words are carved in her heart, is shown to be so; Auden held that in opera what is sung is so.
